en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 9.
The Second Training Rule on What Has Been Set Aside.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain man said to another man:
"I will clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe.
He too spoke thus:
“I too shall clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe.
A certain alms-collecting bhikkhu overheard this conversation between those men.
Then that bhikkhu went to the venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans; having approached him, he said this to the venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans:
“You have great merit, friend Upananda.
In such-and-such a place, a certain man said this to another man:
‘I shall clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe.’”
He also said this:
“I too will clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe. [The other replied:
“Friend, do you have supporters?”
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son approached those men; having approached them, he said to those men:
"Is it true, friends, that you wish to clothe me in robes?
"It is so, noble sir."
“We will clothe the venerable Upananda with robes.
“Friends, if you wish to clothe me with robes, clothe me with such robes as these;
for what shall I do with those which, though they clothe me, I will not use?”
Then those men complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are full of great desires and lack contentment.
It is not easy to clothe them with robes.”
"How can the venerable Upananda, without being previously invited by us, approach us and make a choice regarding a robe?
The monks heard those men grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they grumbled, complained, and expressed their indignation:
“How indeed could the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, without having been previously invited, approach householders and make a request for robes?
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, Upananda, that you, without having been previously invited, approached householders and made a request for robes?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
“Are they your relatives, Upananda, or strangers?
“They are strangers, Blessed One.”
“An unrelated person, foolish man, does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate, or what is good or bad, regarding those who are unrelated.
Yet you, foolish man, having previously been uninvited, have approached unrelated householders and made a request for robe-cloth.
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“If, with reference to a certain monk, separate funds for robes have been set aside by two unrelated householders or housewives, [with the thought]:
‘Having purchased separate robes with these separate funds for robes, we shall clothe the monk named so-and-so with robes’;”
If that bhikkhu, having previously been uninvited, should approach [the donors] and make a choice regarding the robe-cloth,

saying, “It would be good indeed if the venerable ones, having purchased such and such a robe with these funds for individual robes, would clothe me; or both of you together with one [robe],” out of a desire for something fine,
it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
"But having designated a bhikkhu" means:
for the sake of a bhikkhu, making a bhikkhu the object [of their intention], desiring to clothe a bhikkhu.
"Of both" means...
Of two persons.
"Unknown" means not related by the mother’s side or the father’s side, up to the seventh generation on the paternal side.
"Householders" refers to whoever dwell in a house.
"Housewives" refers to...
Whoever lives at home:
"articles for purchasing robes" means gold or silver, pearls, gems, coral, crystal, cloth, thread, or cotton.
"By these means of procuring a robe for an individual" means by those [means] being present.
"Having procured" means:
Having exchanged [them].
"We shall clothe [you]" means we shall give [them] to you.
"In that case, 'that monk' refers to the monk for whose sake the robe-funds have been set aside.
'Without having been invited beforehand' means— "
It was not said before: "Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you need? What kind of robe should we have made for you?
"Having approached" means having gone to the house, or having approached anywhere at all.
"To make a choice regarding the robe" means:
"Whether it be long, or wide, or fine, or soft—
with these individual robe-funds."
By those things present.
"Of such a kind or such a kind" means long,
or broad, or thick, or fine.
"Cetāpetvā" means having exchanged.
"Acchādetha" means clothe [them].
One should give.
"Both together with one" means two persons with one [person].
"Out of a desire for what is good" means:
one who seeks excellence, one who seeks high value.
If, by his word, they cause [the robe] to be obtained as long, wide, thick, or fine, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of procurement.
By the mere acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:

…pe… “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which I had approached unrelated householders with whom I was not previously invited to ask for, and which has become an object of deliberation regarding its form, is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. …pe…
"Should give," ... "should give," ... "I give to the Venerable One."

If, regarding one who is unrelated, he perceives them as unrelated, and having approached householders without being previously invited, he makes a request concerning a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).

If, regarding one who is unrelated, he is doubtful, and having approached householders without being previously invited, he makes a request concerning a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

If, regarding one who is unrelated, he perceives them as related, and having approached householders without being previously invited, he makes a request concerning a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is doubtful regarding a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
in the case of relatives,
or when invited.
For the sake of another,
one exchanges something of little value for something of great value using one's own wealth, desiring to acquire the more expensive item.
"Of one who is insane,
of a first-offender"—
thus ends the ninth training rule concerning what has been prepared for a second time.
